title: Encode and Decode Strings
hints: any single-character delimiter can appear inside one of the strings themselves, which breaks a naive split-on-delimiter decode - you need a scheme where the delimiter's meaning can never be ambiguous
what if, right before each string, you wrote down how many characters long it is?
encode each string as '<length>#<string>', e.g. "3#cat", and concatenate all of these with no separator needed between entries
to decode, scan for the next '#', parse everything before it as a number (the length), then read exactly that many characters as the next string, and repeat from there

this works no matter what characters are inside the string, including more '#' characters or digits, because you never search for content inside the string itself - you always know its exact length up front
commonMistakes: using a single reserved delimiter character to join strings, which breaks when an element contains that exact character
decoding by splitting on '#' instead of reading exactly <length> characters after it, which breaks when the string content itself contains '#'
off-by-one errors when slicing out the length-prefixed substring, especially forgetting to advance the read position past both the length digits and the '#' separator
not handling the empty list or empty-string elements as a valid special case

content.problemStatement:
Design an encode function that takes a list of strings and joins them into
one single string, and a matching decode function that takes that single
string and recovers the exact original list, in order. The strings can
contain any characters at all, including digits, the `#` character, or
sequences that look like your own encoding format, so a naive
join-with-a-delimiter scheme is not safe. For this exercise, the list is
given to you as a single input string `strs`, with elements separated by
`"|"`.

**Encode the resulting list with your own scheme, then immediately decode what you just encoded, and return the recovered list re-joined the same way, with `"|"` between elements.**

An empty `strs` means an empty list, and two adjacent `"|"` characters mean an empty-string element sits between them.
constraints: 0 <= number of strings in the list <= 200
strings may contain any characters, including digits and '#', except the '|' used by this exercise's input/output transport format
notes: the empty list (strs is the empty string)
a list containing one or more empty-string elements
an element that itself contains digits followed by '#', mimicking the encoding format
an element made entirely of '#' characters

sampleTestCases.explanation: encoding "cat" and "dog" with a length-prefix scheme like "3#cat3#dog" and decoding it back recovers ["cat", "dog"] exactly
the element "4#dog" looks like it could confuse a naive decoder, but a length-prefix scheme reads exactly 5 characters for it regardless of what they are, recovering it intact
the list ["", "a", ""] round-trips correctly, including the empty-string elements

optimal.time: O(total characters) for both encode and decode
optimal.space: O(total characters) for the encoded string
optimal.pattern: length-prefix encoding - store each string's length before it, followed by a separator, so decode always knows exactly how many characters to read

bruteForce.approach: join elements with a single fixed delimiter character (like a comma), and decode by splitting on it
